title: Experimental KRAS Vaccine Shows Promise in First Human Pancreatic Cancer Prevention Trial
excerpt: A phase 1 trial at Johns Hopkins found the mKRAS-VAX vaccine triggered immune responses in 90% of high-risk participants, with none developing pancreatic cancer after 16.5 months of follow-up.
body:
• The mKRAS-VAX vaccine generated mutant KRAS-targeted immune responses in 18 of 20 high-risk participants (90%), with a median 18.2-fold increase in T-cell activity.
  • After 16.5 months of median follow-up, no vaccinated participants developed pancreatic cancer, and 37.5% saw their precancerous pancreatic cysts shrink or disappear.
  • Vaccine-induced immune memory T cells remained detectable for up to two years after vaccination, a key factor for long-term cancer interception.
  • Researchers at Johns Hopkins have launched a follow-up study to examine how the vaccine affects precancerous pancreatic tissue directly.

An experimental vaccine targeting the genetic mutations that drive most pancreatic cancers safely generated durable immune responses in people at high risk for the disease, according to results from what researchers believe is the first-in-human prevention trial of its kind.

The phase 1 trial, conducted at the Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center and published July 16 in Cancer Discovery, tested a peptide-based vaccine called mKRAS-VAX in 20 participants who carried a hereditary predisposition to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and had a pancreatic abnormality — typically a cyst — detected on imaging. None had been diagnosed with pancreatic cancer at enrollment.

How the Vaccine Works

KRAS gene mutations are present in more than 90% of pancreatic cancers and most precancerous pancreatic lesions. The mKRAS-VAX vaccine targets the six most common KRAS mutations, training the immune system to recognise and destroy cells carrying these mutations before they turn cancerous.

Participants received four doses over 13 weeks — injections at weeks one, three, and five, followed by a booster at week 13. The trial enrolled patients between April 2022 and February 2026.

The results were striking: 18 of 20 participants (90%) developed a significant immune response. The median increase in mutant KRAS-specific T-cell activity was 18.2-fold. Half the participants responded to all six KRAS mutations included in the vaccine. Critically, the vaccine generated both CD4-positive and CD8-positive T cells — one type to attack abnormal cells, another to provide longer-term immune memory — with vaccine-induced T-cell clones remaining detectable for as long as two years.

"This is just the beginning, but the findings suggest that the immune system is getting activated. We have more work to do, but this is a good start aimed at prevention, which no one had thought about doing before."

— Elizabeth Jaffee, M.D., Deputy Director, Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center

Early Signs of Clinical Impact

While the trial was designed to evaluate safety rather than efficacy, the early clinical signals were encouraging. After a median follow-up of 16.5 months, none of the 20 participants developed pancreatic cancer or a high-risk lesion requiring surgery.

In an exploratory imaging analysis, five participants experienced complete radiographic resolution of their pancreatic cysts, while three others saw partial regression. The remaining cysts stayed stable. Overall, 37.5% of vaccinated participants experienced cyst shrinkage or disappearance — notable given that these cysts are considered precursors to PDAC.

The vaccine was well tolerated. All adverse events were mild to moderate, limited to injection-site reactions, fatigue, chills, and flu-like symptoms that resolved without treatment.

"The long-lasting response of this vaccine is particularly noteworthy when assessing for possible interception of cancer, which requires long-lasting immunity," said Neeha Zaidi, M.D., associate professor of oncology at Johns Hopkins and co-senior author of the study. "This study represents the first proof of concept for the use of vaccines for interception of pancreatic cancer in human patients."

A Deadly Cancer With Few Early Detection Options

Pancreatic cancer remains one of the most lethal malignancies. In the United States alone, approximately 60,000 people are diagnosed annually, and about 50,000 die from the disease each year, according to recent estimates. The five-year survival rate for metastatic PDAC is approximately 3%, largely because most cases are diagnosed at an advanced stage due to the absence of early symptoms and reliable screening tools.

The cancer typically develops over many years from precursor lesions such as pancreatic cysts, which creates a potential window for preventive intervention — precisely the approach the Johns Hopkins team is pursuing.

The mKRAS-VAX vaccine was first tested in 2020 in patients who had undergone surgery and were at high risk of cancer recurrence. A study published in Nature Communications in 2026 found that patients who mounted a strong immune response to the vaccine remained disease-free for at least five years — results that prompted the current prevention trial.

"We thought if we can see an immune response in patients with cancer, the vaccine should work even better in people who are at higher risk because of a family history, gene alteration or cyst on the pancreas."

— Neeha Zaidi, M.D., Associate Professor of Oncology, Johns Hopkins

What's Next

The researchers caution that the small sample size and relatively short follow-up period limit conclusions about clinical efficacy. Larger, longer studies are needed to confirm whether the vaccine actually prevents pancreatic cancer.

The Johns Hopkins team has already initiated an additional study examining the vaccine's effects in patients with high-risk pancreatic cysts undergoing surgical resection. That trial will allow researchers to directly observe how vaccine-induced immune cells interact with precancerous tissue.

The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute, Stand Up To Cancer, and the Lustgarten Foundation. Several study authors, including Jaffee and Zaidi, hold equity in Adventris Pharmaceuticals, which has licensed the vaccine technology from Johns Hopkins University.

"The ability to vaccinate people at risk early to try to prevent them from developing cancer in the future is an important opportunity," Jaffee said. "More studies are needed to find the best vaccine approaches, the best targets and the ideal timing for vaccination."
image_caption: An experimental vaccine targeting the KRAS gene mutation shows early promise in preventing pancreatic cancer in high-risk patients
nri_angle: The vaccine's preventive approach holds particular relevance for Indian-Americans and diaspora families monitoring hereditary cancer risks, as pancreatic cancer incidence continues to rise globally and early intervention options have been scarce.
